newsitem.title: MALTA: Europeans fail to overcome Middle East impasse.
newsitem.headline: Europeans fail to overcome Middle East impasse.

text.p: The gulf between Palestinians and Israelis appeared as wide as ever after intensive European efforts to get the two sides to talk in Malta.

Palestinian officials said EU efforts to bring Palestinian President Yasser Arafat into talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy had foundered despite separate meetings with the two men by 15 European ministers.

"The chances of a meeting between Mr Levy and the President almost do not exist. The President is not going to meet with Mr Levy because of certain issues that need to be discussed," Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani told Reuters.
Kanafani said even a meeting between Levy and a Palestinian minister now looked unlikely.
"There was a quasi-agreement that Levy would meet a Palestinian minister. The president authorised a meeting. Now there has been a retraction on this position," he said.
Earlier, Palestinian Planning Minister Nabil Shaath said he would meet Levy.
As the European diplomatic effort was underway on Tuesday, Washington announced it was sending its special envoy Dennis Ross back to the Middle East for another attempt at resolving the impasse.

Levy and Arafat were in Malta for an EU-Mediterranean meeting which was supposed to focus on laying the groundwork for a Charter for Peace and Stability in the region, promote a regional free trade area and further social and cultural links.
But throughout preparation by officials on Malta, and then in ministers' statements to the conference, the month-old crisis in the Middle East peace process dominated.

In recognition of this the conference chairman, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, gave extra time to the Palestinians and Israelis to put their views, and also to Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf as spokesman for the Arab group.

In his speech, Levy urged the Palestinians to resume negotiations without conditions. But he did not refer to the building of a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem which Palestinians say provoked the crisis and almost daily violence.
Diplomats say the Palestinians want some Israeli gesture.

Kanafani told Reuters: "We have no objection in principle to meeting the Israelis if the subject to be discussed is the crisis we suffer from and attempts to solve this crisis and put the peace process back on the right track."

Arafat and Levy had briefly shaken hands during a reception hosted by Maltese Prime Minister Alfred Sant. It was the highest level contact since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the go-ahead for the settlement.
But the rancour returned as Arafat and Levy addressed the conference.

"With the current Israeli government we have faced many obstacles and impediments," Arafat said. "Instead of continuing to build and reinforce fruitful cooperation and mutual respect ... the Israeli government continues its settlement policy.
"We have been running around in closed circles without reaching any kind of positive agreement."

In response, Levy appealed for "the Palestinian Authority to broadcast, to publicise an unequivocally clear message against terrorism, refuting terrorism, returning to the dialogue, making the peace objective a common goal"
Nine delegates, including Syria, had still to speak when the meeting adjourned to Wednesday morning.
Senior Arab officials met earlier on Tuesday and Algeria's foreign minister Attaf said they wanted a reference to the Middle East stalemate in the final statement.
EU officials said they would try avoid this.
